title: Constructions & Loci
description: Using a ruler and compasses to construct triangles, perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors and simple loci.

notes.heading: Constructing a Triangle from Three Sides (SSS)

illustration.alt: Construction of the perpendicular bisector of a line segment using intersecting arcs.
illustration.caption: Intersecting arcs from A and B locate points through which the perpendicular bisector passes.

notes.body:
📌 Definition
A construction is an accurate drawing made with a ruler and compasses. When we construct a triangle, all construction arcs must be left visible to show how the vertices were found.

🔑 Key Concept
If the lengths of all three sides are known, the triangle can be drawn using the SSS construction method. The three sides fix the shape and size of the triangle.

💡 Worked Example
Construct triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 6\text{ cm}$, $BC = 5\text{ cm}$ and $CA = 4\text{ cm}$.

Step 1: Draw side $AB = 6\text{ cm}$ with a ruler.
Step 2: Set the compass to $4\text{ cm}$. With centre $A$, draw an arc above $AB$.
Step 3: Set the compass to $5\text{ cm}$. With centre $B$, draw an arc that crosses the first arc at $C$.
Step 4: Join $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $C$ with the ruler.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Leave all construction arcs visible.
• The two arcs from $A$ and $B$ must intersect; if they do not, the given lengths cannot form a triangle.
• Always check each side with a ruler.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Rubbing out the construction arcs. Arcs are part of the method and must be shown to earn method marks.

✅ Check
Measure the three sides: they should be $6\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$.

notes.heading: Perpendicular Bisector of a Line Segment
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A perpendicular bisector is a straight line that cuts a line segment exactly in half and meets it at $90^\circ$.

🔑 Key Concept
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$ is the same distance from $A$ and from $B$. This is why the construction uses equal radii from both ends.

💡 Worked Example
Construct the perpendicular bisector of line segment $AB$.

Step 1: Open the compass to a radius greater than half of $AB$.
Step 2: With centre $A$, draw arcs above and below $AB$.
Step 3: With centre $B$ and the same radius, draw arcs above and below $AB$ that cross the first arcs.
Step 4: Join the two crossing points with a straight line. This line is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The compass must be opened to more than half the length of the segment.
• The bisector passes through the midpoint of $AB$.
• It meets $AB$ at exactly $90^\circ$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using a radius smaller than half of $AB$. The arcs will not cross, so the bisector cannot be drawn.

✅ Check
Measure the two parts of $AB$; they should be equal, and the angle at the midpoint should be $90^\circ$.

notes.heading: Angle Bisector
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An angle bisector is a straight line that splits an angle into two equal, smaller angles.

🔑 Key Concept
Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the two arms of the angle. The construction makes two pairs of equal arcs to guarantee this property.

💡 Worked Example
Bisect angle $ABC$.

Step 1: With the compass point on $B$, draw an arc that crosses both arms of the angle. Label the crossings $P$ and $Q$.
Step 2: With the compass point on $P$ and then on $Q$, draw two arcs inside the angle using the same radius. Let them cross at $R$.
Step 3: Draw a straight line from $B$ through $R$. This line bisects angle $ABC$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Keep the compass width the same for both inner arcs.
• The bisector always starts from the vertex of the angle.
• Each half-angle is equal to the original angle divided by two.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Changing the compass width between the two inner arcs. Different radii make the crossing point wrong, so the bisector will not split the angle exactly in half.

✅ Check
Measure the two new angles; they should be equal.

notes.heading: Shortest Distance from a Point to a Line
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The perpendicular distance from a point to a line is the shortest distance between them. The line joining the point to the line meets the line at $90^\circ$.

🔑 Key Concept
Out of all possible line segments from a point to a line, the perpendicular one is the shortest. Any other segment would be the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.

💡 Worked Example
Construct the perpendicular from point $P$ to line $AB$.

Step 1: With centre $P$, draw an arc that cuts line $AB$ at two points, $X$ and $Y$.
Step 2: With centres $X$ and $Y$ and the same radius, draw arcs on the opposite side of $AB$ from $P$ that cross at $Q$.
Step 3: Join $P$ to $Q$. The line $PQ$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The perpendicular gives the shortest distance from the point to the line.
• Construction arcs must cross the original line in two places.
• The final line meets the original line at $90^\circ$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Joining the point to the nearest end of the line instead of drawing a perpendicular. This usually gives a longer distance.

✅ Check
Measure the angle where $PQ$ meets $AB$; it should be $90^\circ$.

notes.heading: Constructing a Triangle from SAS
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A triangle can be constructed when two side lengths and the angle between them are known. This is called the SAS case: Side-Angle-Side.

🔑 Key Concept
The angle must be the included angle between the two known sides. Draw one side, construct the given angle at one end, then mark off the second side length along the new ray.

💡 Worked Example
Construct triangle $PQR$ with $QR = 5\text{ cm}$, angle $PQR = 50^\circ$ and $PQ = 7\text{ cm}$.

Step 1: Draw side $QR = 5\text{ cm}$.
Step 2: At $Q$, construct an angle of $50^\circ$ and draw a ray from $Q$.
Step 3: Measure $7\text{ cm}$ along the ray and mark point $P$.
Step 4: Join $P$ to $R$ to complete the triangle.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The known angle must sit between the two known sides.
• Use a protractor or a construction to make the angle accurately.
• Leave any construction arcs visible.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Placing the known angle at the wrong vertex, so the two given sides do not meet at the correct angle.

✅ Check
Measure sides $QR$, $PQ$ and angle $PQR$; they should be $5\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$ and $50^\circ$.

notes.heading: Constructing a Triangle from ASA
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A triangle can be constructed when two angles and the side between them are known. This is called the ASA case: Angle-Side-Angle.

🔑 Key Concept
The known side must lie between the two known angles. Draw the side first, then construct each angle at the two endpoints. The point where the new rays meet is the third vertex.

💡 Worked Example
Construct triangle $XYZ$ with $XY = 6\text{ cm}$, angle $YXZ = 40^\circ$ and angle $XYZ = 70^\circ$.

Step 1: Draw side $XY = 6\text{ cm}$.
Step 2: At $X$, construct an angle of $40^\circ$ and draw a ray.
Step 3: At $Y$, construct an angle of $70^\circ$ and draw a ray.
Step 4: The point where the two rays cross is $Z$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The given side must be between the two given angles.
• The third angle can be found because angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$.
• The two new rays must cross to form the triangle.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing the two given angles on the same side of the known side so that the rays diverge and never meet.

✅ Check
The three angles should add to $180^\circ$; here $40^\circ + 70^\circ + 70^\circ = 180^\circ$.

notes.heading: Simple Loci
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A locus (plural loci) is the set of all points that satisfy a given rule. It describes the path of a moving point.

🔑 Key Concept
Recognising the rule helps you name the locus:
• Equidistant from a fixed point: a circle.
• Equidistant from two fixed points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
• Equidistant from a straight line: two parallel lines, one on each side.
• Equidistant from two intersecting lines: the pair of angle bisectors.

💡 Worked Example
Describe the locus of points that are $3\text{ cm}$ from point $O$.

The rule says the distance from the point to $O$ is always $3\text{ cm}$. The locus is therefore a circle with centre $O$ and radius $3\text{ cm}$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A locus is a path or set of points, not a single point.
• Use a compass to draw circular loci.
• Use perpendicular bisectors for two points and angle bisectors for two lines.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that the locus of points a fixed distance from a straight line is two parallel lines, one on each side of the line.

✅ Check
State the rule and then match it to one of the common loci.

questions.stem: Which information is needed to construct a unique triangle using the SSS method?
questions.explanation: SSS needs the lengths of all three sides; these fix the triangle's size and shape uniquely.

questions.stem: What is the first step in constructing the perpendicular bisector of a line segment?
choices: Draw a line through the midpoint
Open the compass to more than half the segment length
Measure the angle with a protractor
Mark the endpoints with a ruler
questions.explanation: The compass must be wider than half the segment so the arcs from both endpoints intersect.

questions.stem: A point lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Which statement is true?
choices: It is closer to $A$ than to $B$
It forms a right angle at $A$
questions.explanation: Any point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from both endpoints of the segment.

questions.stem: What does an angle bisector do?
choices: Cuts the opposite side in half
Splits an angle into two equal angles
Makes a right angle with the vertex
Doubles the size of the angle
questions.explanation: An angle bisector divides the original angle into two congruent smaller angles.

questions.stem: Which instrument is used to draw construction arcs and circles?
questions.explanation: A compass keeps a fixed radius and is used to draw arcs and circles.

questions.stem: Which locus is the set of points equidistant from a single fixed point?
questions.explanation: A circle is the path of all points at a fixed distance from its centre.

questions.stem: Which locus is the set of points equidistant from two fixed points?
choices: The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them
A line parallel to the segment
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector contains all points that are the same distance from both endpoints.

questions.stem: A point moves so that it is always the same distance from two intersecting lines. What is its locus?
questions.explanation: The angle bisectors contain all points equidistant from the two lines; there are two bisectors for two intersecting lines.

questions.stem: How is the shortest distance from a point to a straight line measured?
choices: Along any slanted line to the line
Along the perpendicular from the point to the line
From the point to the nearest endpoint
By drawing a circle through the point
questions.explanation: The perpendicular segment from the point to the line is the shortest possible distance.

questions.stem: A triangle is constructed from two sides and the included angle. Which method is being used?
questions.explanation: SAS stands for Side-Angle-Side, where the angle is between the two known sides.

questions.stem: A triangle is constructed from two angles and the side between them. Which method is being used?
questions.explanation: ASA stands for Angle-Side-Angle, with the known side between the two known angles.

questions.stem: A triangle has angles $40^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ and the side between them is $6\text{ cm}$. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so the third angle is $180^\circ - 40^\circ - 70^\circ = 70^\circ$.

questions.stem: A point moves so it is always $4\text{ cm}$ from a straight line. What is its locus?
questions.explanation: There are two lines, one on each side of the given line, each $4\text{ cm}$ away from it.

questions.stem: Which error makes an angle bisector construction inaccurate?
choices: Drawing the first arc too large
Changing the compass width between the two inner arcs
questions.explanation: The two inner arcs must be drawn with the same radius so their crossing point is on the true bisector.

questions.stem: Why must construction arcs be left visible?
choices: They show the method used to find the result
They are required only for circles
questions.explanation: Visible arcs allow the reader to see how the construction was done and are needed for method marks.

questions.stem: A triangle is constructed using the lengths of all three sides. Which construction method is this?
questions.explanation: SSS stands for Side-Side-Side: all three side lengths are known, and they fix the triangle uniquely.

questions.stem: While constructing the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, a student opens the compass to less than half of $AB$. What goes wrong?
choices: The angle at the midpoint is not $90^\circ$
The midpoint is in the wrong place
The arcs from $A$ and $B$ do not cross, so the bisector cannot be drawn
questions.explanation: The compass must be opened to more than half the segment so the arcs from the two endpoints intersect. With a smaller radius the arcs never meet.

questions.stem: Point $R$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$, and $RP = 9\text{ cm}$. What is $RQ$?
questions.explanation: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the two endpoints, so $RQ = RP = 9\text{ cm}$.

questions.stem: An angle of $76^\circ$ is split by its angle bisector. How big is each of the two new angles?
questions.explanation: An angle bisector halves the angle: $76^\circ \div 2 = 38^\circ$. Choice C halves it twice; choice B doubles it.

questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the size of an angle after it has been constructed?
questions.explanation: A protractor measures angles in degrees. The compass and ruler draw the construction; the protractor checks the result.

questions.stem: Describe the locus of points that are exactly $5\text{ cm}$ from a fixed point $C$.
choices: The perpendicular bisector of a segment from $C$
The bisectors of the angles at $C$
A circle with centre $C$ and radius $5\text{ cm}$
questions.explanation: A circle is the set of all points at a fixed distance from its centre, so the locus is a circle of radius $5\text{ cm}$ around $C$.

questions.stem: A dog moves so that it is always the same distance from two posts $P$ and $Q$. What is the locus of the dog?
choices: A circle around the midpoint of $PQ$
questions.explanation: Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.

questions.stem: A path is designed so that every point on it is the same distance from two straight fences that cross each other. What is the locus of the path?
choices: The pair of angle bisectors of the angles between the fences
questions.explanation: Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on the angle bisectors. Two crossing lines have two bisectors, one for each pair of angles.

questions.stem: Which segment gives the shortest distance from a point $P$ to a line $l$?
choices: The segment from $P$ to the nearest endpoint of $l$
The segment from $P$ to the midpoint of $l$
questions.explanation: The shortest distance from a point to a line is always measured along the perpendicular, which meets the line at $90^\circ$.

questions.stem: A triangle is constructed from a side of $8\text{ cm}$ with angles of $35^\circ$ and $65^\circ$ drawn at its two ends. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: ASA stands for Angle-Side-Angle: the known side lies between the two known angles, and the two rays meet at the third vertex.

questions.stem: A triangle has angles $55^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ at the two ends of a given side. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so the third angle is $180^\circ - 55^\circ - 60^\circ = 65^\circ$. Choice B just adds the two given angles.

questions.stem: A point moves so that it is always $2\text{ cm}$ from a long straight rail. What is its locus?
choices: One line parallel to the rail
The perpendicular bisector of the rail
Two lines parallel to the rail, one on each side
questions.explanation: The point can be $2\text{ cm}$ from the rail on either side, so the locus is two parallel lines, each $2\text{ cm}$ away. Choice A forgets the second side.

questions.stem: In an angle bisector construction, the first arc from the vertex crosses the arms at $P$ and $Q$. What must be true of the two arcs drawn from $P$ and $Q$?
choices: They must be drawn with the same compass radius
They must have radius equal to $PQ$
They must be smaller than half of $PQ$
questions.explanation: Equal radii from $P$ and $Q$ make the crossing point equidistant from both arms, which is exactly what places it on the true bisector.

questions.stem: After constructing a triangle, a student rubs out all the construction arcs. Why is this a problem?
choices: The triangle disappears with the arcs
The arcs show how the vertices were found — rubbing them out loses the method marks
The ruler can no longer measure the sides
questions.explanation: Construction arcs are the evidence of the method. Examiners award method marks for correct arcs, so they must be left visible.
